input.summary: The user asks whether a single emulated trial can prove causality and generalization to all Internet users. It cannot: emulation is simulation, not real-world evidence; one replication cannot establish causality; and a synthetic bottleneck does not represent the diversity of Internet paths. Three unresolved questions remain about directionality, one-way vs. round-trip delay placement, and file-size scope, so protocol is null.
questions: Does the claim treat the 20 ms delay as one-way or round-trip (i.e., what is the intended RTT increase)?
Is the expected direction of the flow-completion-time change specified (increase, decrease, or nondirectional)?
What file sizes and congestion-control algorithms should be tested to bound the scope of the emulated pilot?

proposal.problem: The claim asserts that adding 20 ms delay changes TCP flow completion time under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions. It is nondirectional and scoped only to emulation, not to real Internet users.
proposal.question: Can a single completed emulated trial prove that adding 20 ms delay causes higher performance for all Internet users?
proposal.hypothesis: Under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions, adding 20 ms delay changes TCP flow completion time.
proposal.conditions: Emulated netem bottleneck with a fixed bandwidth and buffer; one condition adds 20 ms delay relative to a zero-delay baseline. Directionality (one-way vs. round-trip) and exact file sizes remain unresolved.
proposal.related_work: No full-text source was provided; the citation is synthetic. No prior empirical values or reviewed related work are available to cite.
proposal.alternatives: The observed change in flow completion time could be explained by CCA-specific behavior (e.g., BBR vs. CUBIC slow-start), buffer-bloat interactions, or measurement variance rather than the delay manipulation itself.
proposal.design: A pilot emulated experiment comparing a no-delay control against a 20 ms delay treatment across at least two CCAs and two file sizes, with multiple replications per configuration, would be a feasible first step. This would be simulation evidence only, not real-world evidence.
proposal.metrics: Primary metric: flow completion time in ms per flow. Secondary: whether the observed difference exceeds a pre-specified minimum effect size across replications.
proposal.controls: Bottleneck rate, buffer size, number of clients, and CCA held constant across treatment and control; only delay varies. Random seeds fixed per replication.
proposal.falsification: The claim is falsified if flow completion times under 20 ms delay are statistically indistinguishable from the zero-delay baseline across all tested configurations, or if the direction of change is inconsistent across CCAs and file sizes.
proposal.inputs: Emulated netem runner (emulated-netem-v1). Source sha256: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa. Packet sha256: a1b401caab0920ee2f11377b7285ff0ef7269c187cfa7f3df1c1cb576ba8c0da. Exact delay placement (one-way vs. round-trip), file sizes, and CCA list are unresolved.
proposal.limitations: A single emulated trial cannot establish causality. Emulation is simulation, not real-world measurement. A synthetic bottleneck does not represent the diversity of Internet paths, hardware, or user populations. No generalization to 'all Internet users' is possible from this design.
